heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > NCD Risk Factors
text:
### NCD risk factors: non-modifiable and modifiable, with clinical relevance

| Category | Risk factor | Clinical relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-modifiable | Age | Risk increases significantly after age 40, especially for DM and HTN. |
| Non-modifiable | Gender | Specific risks (e.g., gender-specific cancers, cardiovascular disease patterns). |
| Non-modifiable | Family history | Genetic predisposition to HTN, DM, or premature coronary artery disease (CAD). |
| Modifiable | Overweight/obesity | High BMI is a primary driver for HTN and DM. |
| Modifiable | Tobacco use (smoking) | A leading preventable cause of cardiovascular and chronic respiratory diseases and lung cancer. |
| Modifiable | Alcohol use | Increases risk of liver disease, some cancers, and hypertension. |
| Modifiable | Unhealthy diet | High intake of salt, sugar, and saturated fats contributes to hypertension and dyslipidaemia and some cancers. |
| Modifiable | Lack of physical activity | A sedentary lifestyle is a key independent risk factor for all major NCDs. |

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Screening for and Identifying Modifiable Risk Factors > Screening protocol: initial assessment for all patients
text:
### Screening protocol for modifiable NCD risk factors: screening method and frequency (initial assessment, all patients)

Target population for screening: all adults aged 18 years and above attending health facilities; priority screening for adults ≥40 years or those with risk factors; pregnant women (at first antenatal visit); people living with HIV (at each clinic visit).

| Risk factor | Screening method | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tobacco use | Ask all patients about current and past tobacco use | Every visit |
| Alcohol use | AUDIT-C questionnaire (3 questions) | Annually |
| Physical activity | Ask: 'How many days per week do you engage in moderate physical activity for at least 30 minutes?' | Annually |
| Diet assessment | Ask about fruit/vegetable intake and consumption of processed foods | Annually |
| Weight/BMI | Measure height and weight; calculate BMI | Every visit |
| Blood pressure | Measure BP using standardized technique | Every visit |
| Blood glucose | Random or fasting blood glucose; HbA1c if available | Age ≥18 years: every visit; high risk: annually |
| Cholesterol | Total cholesterol; LDL/HDL if available | Screening guidelines for lipid disorders differ among experts. Cholesterol screening is recommended in adult men aged ≥35 years, in women aged ≥40 years or menopausal, and all adults with any risk factors. |

text:
### BMI classification and recommended action

| BMI (kg/m2) | Classification | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <18.5 | Underweight | Nutritional assessment; screen for underlying conditions |
| 18.5-24.9 | Normal weight | Encourage maintenance; promote healthy lifestyle |
| 25.0-29.9 | Overweight | Lifestyle counselling; 5-10% weight loss goal |
| 30.0-34.9 | Obesity class I | Intensive lifestyle intervention; screen for comorbidities |
| 35.0-39.9 | Obesity class II | As above; consider referral for specialist care |
| ≥40 | Obesity class III (severe) | Refer to specialist; multidisciplinary approach |

text:
### Blood pressure screening algorithm: BP categories and actions

| BP reading (mmHg) | Category | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <120/80 | Normal | Recheck in 1 year or at next clinic visit, whichever comes first; promote healthy lifestyle |
| 120-129/<80 | Elevated | Lifestyle modification; recheck in 3-6 months |
| 130-139/80-89 | Stage 1 hypertension | Confirm with 2 more readings; initiate lifestyle + medication if CVD risk ≥10% |
| ≥140/90 | Stage 2 hypertension | Confirm within 1 month; initiate lifestyle + medication |
| ≥180/120 | Hypertensive crisis | URGENT: assess for end-organ damage; immediate treatment |

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Referral Criteria and Follow-Up > Follow-up schedule
text:
### Follow-up schedule for NCD risk conditions (initial and stable follow-up)

Non-urgent referral: uncontrolled BP on 3 medications at optimal doses; diabetes uncontrolled (HbA1c >9%) despite dual therapy; secondary hypertension suspected (young age, resistant hypertension); complications of diabetes (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy); BMI ≥40, or BMI ≥35 with significant comorbidities; severe alcohol dependence (AUDIT score >20).

| Condition | Initial follow-up | Stable follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Newly diagnosed hypertension | 2-4 weeks after starting medication | Every 3-6 months when controlled |
| Newly diagnosed diabetes | Monthly until stable | Every 3 months (HbA1c check) |
| Pre-diabetes | 3 months (lifestyle counselling) | Every 6-12 months |
| Overweight/obesity | Monthly for first 3 months | Every 3-6 months |
| Tobacco cessation | 1-2 weeks after quit date | Monthly for 6 months, then as needed |

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Physical Inactivity > WHO physical activity recommendations
text:
### WHO physical activity recommendations by age group (children, adults, older adults, pregnant and postpartum women)

Physical inactivity: not meeting the WHO recommendation of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. Sedentary behaviour: any waking behaviour with low energy expenditure (≤1.5 METs) while sitting, reclining, or lying down.

| Age group | Recommendations |
| --- | --- |
| Children & adolescents (5-17 years) | At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous intensity PA daily. Include vigorous-intensity aerobic activities at least 3 days/week. Include muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 days/week. |
| Adults (18-64 years) | At least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity PA per week, OR at least 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity PA per week, OR an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous activity. Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week. |
| Older adults (≥65 years) | Same as adults (150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous). Muscle-strengthening activities 2 or more days per week. Multicomponent PA emphasizing functional balance and strength training 3 or more days/week to prevent falls. |
| Pregnant & postpartum women | At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity PA per week. Incorporate a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities. Add gentle stretching; may be beneficial to add pelvic floor muscle training. |

**Note:** Note: some activity is better than none. Inactive individuals should start with small amounts and gradually increase frequency, intensity, and duration. Screening for physical inactivity: who to screen: all patients attending primary care facilities, particularly those with risk factors (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression); routine screening at annual check-ups or chronic disease reviews.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Physical Inactivity > Brief counselling intervention (5 A's framework)
text:
### Brief counselling intervention for physical inactivity: the 5 A's (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange)

Screening: if <150 minutes of moderate activity per week, the patient is physically inactive.

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| ASK | Ask about current physical activity levels using screening questions. |
| ADVISE | Provide clear, personalized advice on benefits of physical activity for their specific health condition. |
| ASSESS | Assess willingness and readiness to change. Identify barriers (time, safety, cost, cultural factors). |
| ASSIST | Help develop a realistic action plan. Start small and build gradually. Provide written guidance. |
| ARRANGE | Arrange follow-up to monitor progress and provide ongoing support. |

doc_title: Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)
heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Nicotine Use > Smoking cessation approach
text:
### Smoking cessation approach in clinical practice (flowchart, with nicotine dependence table)

All smokers should be identified and their readiness to quit evaluated. If resistance to quitting exists, information and suitable follow-up should be provided. If the person is ready to make a quit attempt, evaluation of nicotine dependence, co-morbid and psychosocial factors should guide the choice of effective interventions.

1. Ask: do you smoke? do you know the risks? have you thought of quitting?
2. Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting? do you know that we can help you?
3. Assess: are you ready to quit?
4. Assist/arrange:
   - No or maybe: give a motivational pamphlet and encourage follow-up; return to Ask at the next visit.
   - Yes: arrange for cessation intervention.
5. Specific nicotine dependence review: Fagerstrom/CO levels; current smoking and history of quit attempts; social stressors/household smokers.
   Dependence level (already attempted to quit / cigarettes per day / time to first cigarette after waking):
   - Very high: yes / >30 / >5 min (printed)
   - High: yes / 20-30 / 5-30 min
   - Medium: yes / 10-20 / 30-60 min
   - Low: no / <10 / >60 min
6. By dependence:
   - Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.
   - Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.
7. Set quit date: arrange appropriate support and medication if needed.
8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.

   - Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.
   - Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.

8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.

text:
### Brief intervention for alcohol use: the 5 A's (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange)

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| ASK | Ask about alcohol use using AUDIT-C: 'How often do you drink alcohol?' 'How much do you typically drink?' |
| ADVISE | Provide clear, personalized advice: 'The safest choice is to not drink alcohol at all. There is no safe level of drinking.' Link to their health concerns: 'Alcohol is making your blood pressure worse' or 'Drinking increases your cancer risk.' |
| ASSESS | Assess readiness to change: 'How do you feel about quitting or cutting down?' 'What makes it difficult for you to stop?' |
| ASSIST | Help develop a quit/reduction plan: set a quit date or reduction goal; identify triggers and develop coping strategies; provide written educational materials; consider referral to counselling or support groups. |
| ARRANGE | Schedule follow-up in 2-4 weeks to monitor progress, provide support, and address challenges. |

### AUDIT-C alcohol screening questionnaire: questions, scoring and interpretation

| Question | Answer scoring | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. How often do you have a drink containing alcohol? | Never (0); monthly or less (1); 2-4 times/month (2); 2-3 times/week (3); 4+ times/week (4) | 0-4 |
| 2. How many drinks containing alcohol do you have on a typical day when drinking? | 1 or 2 (0); 3 or 4 (1); 5 or 6 (2); 7-9 (3); 10+ (4) | 0-4 |
| 3. How often do you have 5 or more drinks on one occasion? | Never (0); less than monthly (1); monthly (2); weekly (3); daily/almost daily (4) | 0-4 |

**Note:** AUDIT-C interpretation: men: score ≥4 = unhealthy alcohol use: provide brief intervention. Women: score ≥3 = unhealthy alcohol use: provide brief intervention. Score ≥8: possible alcohol use disorder: consider full AUDIT and referral.

text:
> **Key messages for patients about alcohol**
>
> - NO amount of alcohol is safe for your health.
> - The safest choice is NOT to drink alcohol at all.
> - Alcohol increases your risk of cancer, heart disease, liver disease, and many other conditions.
> - Quitting alcohol improves your health at any age.
> - You don't have to quit alone: ask for help from healthcare providers, family, and support groups.
> - If you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, do NOT drink any alcohol.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Unhealthy Diet > Healthy eating guidelines
text:
### Healthy eating guidelines: food groups, foods to limit, counselling tips and health benefits

**Eat a variety of foods daily for good health**

| Food group | Advice | Details / examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vegetables & fruits | Eat PLENTY daily | At least 5 portions (400 g) per day. Examples: spinach, cabbage, tomatoes, carrots, pumpkin, oranges, bananas, mangoes |
| Starchy foods | Part of MOST meals | Choose WHOLE GRAINS. Examples: whole grain pap/maize meal, brown bread, rice, potatoes, sweet potatoes |
| Protein foods | Eat DAILY | Choose lean options. Examples: beans, lentils, peanuts, fish, chicken, lean meat, eggs |
| Milk & dairy | Have EVERY DAY | Good for bones & teeth. Examples: milk, maas, yoghurt, cheese |
| Clean water | Drink LOTS daily | 6-8 glasses per day; best choice for hydration |
| Fats & oils | Use SPARINGLY | Choose vegetable oils; avoid hard fats & excessive frying |

**Foods to limit**

| Food group | Advice | Details / examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salt | Less than 1 teaspoon (5 g) per day | Reduces blood pressure & heart disease |
| Sugar | Less than 6 teaspoons (25 g) per day | Reduces blood pressure & heart disease |
| Processed foods | Limit chips, soda, sweets, fast food | High in salt, sugar & unhealthy fats |

**Note:** Counselling tips: fill half the plate with vegetables; eat locally available seasonal foods; choose whole grains over refined; eat beans/legumes regularly; remove visible fat from meat. Health benefits: prevents heart disease & stroke; reduces diabetes risk; helps maintain a healthy weight; prevents some cancers; improves overall wellbeing.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Hypertension > Algorithm for hypertension screening
text:
### Algorithm for hypertension screening in adults (18 years and above)

Adults (18 years and above), by office blood pressure:
- Optimal <120/80: repeat at least every 5 years.
- Normal 120-129/80-84: repeat at least every 3 years.
- High normal BP 130-139/85-89: consider masked hypertension; repeat annually. Consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).
- Hypertension >140/90: repeated visits for office BP measurement, and consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).

Adopted from ESC/ESH guidelines, 2023.
N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring blood pressure yearly for adults ≥18 years of age.

text:
### Anthropometric measurements in adults (≥18 years): BMI, obesity class and disease risk by waist circumference

Overweight and obesity are abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that presents a risk to health. In adults, a BMI over 25 is overweight and over 30 is obese. BMI = body mass (kg) divided by the square of body height (m).

| Category | BMI (kg/m2) | Obesity class | Disease risk\* (relative to normal weight and waist circumference) Men ≤ 102 cm and women ≤ 88 cm | Disease risk\* (relative to normal weight and waist circumference) Men ≥ 102 cm and women ≥ 88 cm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Underweight | <18.5 |  | - |  |
| Normal\* | 18.5-24.9 |  | - |  |
| Overweight | 25-29.9 |  | Increased | High |
| Obesity | 30-34.9 | Class 1 | High | Very high |
| Obesity | 35-39.9 | Class 2 | Very high | Very high |
| Obesity | ≥ 40 | Class 3 | Extremely high | Extremely high |

*Disease risk for hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases.
*Increased waist circumference can also be a marker for increased risk even in persons of normal weight.

doc_title: Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)
heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Diabetes Mellitus > Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening
text:
### Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening in adults

All clients >18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using the known risk factors below.
- No risk factors: re-evaluate.
- Risk factors present: test (HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, or random glucose):
  - HbA1c <5.7% / FPG <100 mg/dl: encourage healthy lifestyle maintenance; retest at least annually.
  - HbA1c 5.6-6.4% / FPG 100-125 mg/dl / OGTT 140-199 mg/dl: encourage lifestyle modification and retest every 6-12 months.
  - HbA1c ≥ 6.5% / FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl: retest with a different test, and refer for treatment if still positive.

*Known risk factors for diabetes: physical inactivity; family history of diabetes; high-risk race or ethnicity (African, Indian); hypertension (≥ 140/90); HDL-C <35 or triglyceride > 250 mg/dL; history of gestational diabetes or gave birth to a baby ≥4.5 kg; history of heart disease; conditions associated with insulin resistance; polycystic ovary syndrome; malnutrition.

Adapted from the American Diabetes Association Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes. N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring glycaemia yearly in adults ≥ 18 years of age.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD clinical protocol (kidney health check)
text:
### Chronic kidney disease clinical protocol: kidney health check, confirmation and staging

Offer a kidney health check to people with: diabetes; hypertension; established CVD; family history of kidney failure; obesity (BMI ≥30); current or past smoker/vaper; history of AKI aged ≥60 years; high index of suspicion in clients, especially paediatrics, with oedema and recurrent puffiness.

Tests: uACR, eGFR, and trace protein on urine dipstick.
- uACR ≥3 mg/mmol (yes): repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void). CKD if a minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months.
- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m2 (yes): repeat eGFR within 7 days; if ≥20% reduction in eGFR, possible AKI: discuss with nephrologist. Repeat eGFR within 3 months. CKD if a minimum of two eGFRs <60 mL/min/1.73m2 over 3 months.
- No to both: repeat kidney health check (annually if aged ≥18, people with diabetes or hypertension).
If either (and/or) criterion is met: stage CKD with the staging table, using eGFR and uACR results.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Lipids Disorders > Lipid management clinical decision pathway
text:
### Lipid management: clinical decision pathway (CV risk, comorbidities, lipid targets)

Obtain fasting lipids at baseline and annually. Then three parallel assessments, then treat to the target:
1. Calculate and categorize CV risk using the Framingham risk score (mdcalc.com - Framingham Risk Score). Risk categories: low risk < 10%; moderate risk 10%-19%; high risk > 20%.
2. Assess comorbidities: diabetes; CAD; previous CV event; atherosclerosis; aneurysm. *Any = high risk.
3. Determine lipid targets:
   - LDL-C: optimal <100 mg/dL; near or above optimal 100-129 mg/dL; borderline high 130-159 mg/dL; high 160-189 mg/dL; very high ≥190 mg/dL.
   - Total cholesterol: desirable <200 mg/dL; borderline high 200-239 mg/dL; high ≥240 mg/dL.
   - Triglycerides: normal <150 mg/dL; borderline high ≥150-199 mg/dL; high 200-499 mg/dL; very high ≥500 mg/dL.
Then: treat to the target.

doc_title: Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)
heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm for CKD screening
text:
### Algorithm for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening

Target population:
- No markers of risk: do not screen.
- Risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, family history, HIV): screen.

Screen: test (urine dipstick, blood glucose, blood pressure, family history) and measure kidney function (serum creatinine; estimate the eGFR).
Determine if test results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 or presence of albuminuria):
- No: rescreen based on the risks.
- Yes: lifestyle modification (smoking cessation; balanced diet; regular exercise; limit salt intake to <2 g/day); medical treatment (diabetes, BP and lipid control: SGLT2, ACEI/ARB, statins, metformin...); considerations (drug dosing; use of contrast media; CKD complications: anaemia, hyperkalaemia, bone disease, CVD...).
Then: retesting; follow-up visits; referral to nephrology when appropriate.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes > Definition, classification and treatment targets
text:
### Diabetes mellitus: definition, classification and treatment targets

| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Definition | Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance), resulting in increased blood glucose. |
| Classification: common types | 1. Type 1 diabetes: due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood. 2. Type 2 diabetes: due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance. |
| Classification: specific types | Monogenic diabetes syndromes (neonatal diabetes; maturity-onset diabetes of the young). Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis). Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation. |
| Treatment target: HbA1c | HbA1c <7% for most adults. HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycaemia. HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy, or cardiovascular complications. |
| Treatment target: glucose | All clients on treatment should aim for a glycaemia (random or fasting) ranging 5-10 mmol/L. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment
text:
### Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment (flowchart, by HbA1c)

Newly diagnosed type 2 DM patient: check HbA1c. Health promotion for all (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour), individual and group.

By HbA1c at diagnosis:
- HbA1c <7%: lifestyle modification; recheck HbA1c in 6 months.
- HbA1c 7-8% (printed '<7%-8%'): start metformin [note 1]: 1. 500 mg OD; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase dose every 3 months until at goal or maximum tolerated dose.
- HbA1c 8-9.9% (printed '<8%-9.9%'): consider dual therapy: 1. start metformin 500 mg OD and titrate every 2 weeks to a maximum of 2 g if tolerated; 2. add a second drug (sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors).
- HbA1c >10%: consider insulin: consider starting the patient on insulin therapy alone or in combination with metformin (consult physician). Start at low-dose insulin and increase until target reached.

Follow-up after lifestyle modification or metformin:
- HbA1c <7%: 1. continue current medication; 2. recheck HbA1c in 6 months; 3. fasting blood glucose every 3 months.
- HbA1c >7%: 1. add a second OGLA, e.g. sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase the dose of the second agent until glycaemic target reached, or maximum dose. If HbA1c remains >8%, review with physician and consider referral to the diabetes clinic for insulin management.

T2DM diagnosis criteria: 1. FPG > 7.0 mmol/L; 2. random glucose > 11.1 mmol/L; 3. need two positive tests, one must be FBG.
For older patients, it is reasonable to set the HbA1c goal at < 8%.

[note 1] Caution: metformin use in patients with reduced kidney function: 1. do not start new patients on metformin if CrCl < 45 ml/min; 2. continue metformin if already on it and CrCl is 30-45 ml/min, but repeat CrCl in 6 months; 3. stop metformin if CrCl < 30 ml/min.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Oral agents used in the management of type 2 diabetes
text:
### Oral agents used in the management of type 2 diabetes: doses, frequency, side effects and contraindications

**A. Sulphonylureas. Mechanism of action: stimulate the pancreas to release insulin (regardless of time and glucose levels)**

| Name of drug | Minimum dose | Max daily dose | Frequency | Major side effects | Contraindications / use with caution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glibenclamide | 2.5 mg | 15 mg | OD or BD | Hypoglycemia, weight gain, skin rashes | Caution in liver and renal disease |
| Gliclazide MR | 30 mg | 120 mg | OD | Hypoglycemia, weight gain, skin rashes | Pregnancy; caution in liver disease |
| Glimepiride | 1 mg | 4 mg | OD | Hypoglycemia, weight gain, skin rashes | Pregnancy; caution in liver and renal disease |
| Glipizide | 5 mg | 40 mg | OD or BD | Hypoglycemia, weight gain, skin rashes | Pregnancy; caution in liver and renal disease |

**B. Biguanide. Mechanism of action: (i) reduce glucose production in liver; (ii) cause (mild) reduction in peripheral insulin resistance**

| Name of drug | Minimum dose | Max daily dose | Frequency | Major side effects | Contraindications / use with caution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin | 500 mg | 2000 mg | OD or BD | Abdominal pain, nausea, loose bowel motions, lactic acidosis; vitamin B12 deficiency with prolonged use | Renal failure, GFR <30 ml/min; heart failure stage 3 or 4; liver failure |

**C. Thiazolidinediones. Mechanism of action: (i) improved insulin sensitivity in muscle, adipose tissue and liver; (ii) reduce glucose output from liver; (iii) change fat distribution by decreasing visceral fat and increasing peripheral fat**

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes
text:
### Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes (monotherapy to triple therapy and insulin)

| Stage | Regimen | Guidance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monotherapy | Metformin is the drug of first choice at diagnosis. | Continue until contraindicated or not tolerated. If metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated, use gliclazide. For patients with established cardiovascular disease intolerant to metformin, consider SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1RA (under specialist care). |
| Initial dual therapy | Metformin + gliclazide | Consider if the patient has symptomatic hyperglycaemia and HbA1c >9% at diagnosis. Review gliclazide continuation once metformin dose and lifestyle interventions are optimized. |
| Dual therapy | Add a second agent if target not achieved with monotherapy | Options to add: gliclazide, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, or SGLT2 inhibitor. Consider comorbidities, ability to access medicines, and properties of each drug. Fixed-dose combinations (e.g., DPP-4 inhibitor + metformin) may offer compliance and cost advantages. |
| Triple therapy | Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent | Consider if HbA1c is above individualized target (typically <7% for most) with two oral agents. Injectable options: GLP-1RA or basal insulin. Do NOT combine: GLP-1RA with DPP-4 inhibitor; GLP-1RA with SGLT2 inhibitor; pioglitazone with insulin. |
| Triple therapy (insulin) | Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent. | For patients on three oral agents who are still not at target. Other oral agents can be stopped upon initiation of premix insulin. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Indications and timing for insulin
text:
### Insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes: indications, when to initiate, and good practice

Diabetes is a progressive condition, and many patients with type 2 diabetes eventually require and benefit from insulin therapy.

| Indications for insulin | When should insulin be initiated? | Good practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Poor glycaemic control: HbA1c still [above target] despite previous attempts to improve with lifestyle modification and maximum oral therapy. Patient is symptomatic (weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections). Steroid-induced diabetes. Patient unable to tolerate or has contraindication to OGLAs. Gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy not controlled on OGLAs. Painful neuropathy. Foot ulceration and infection. | As soon as there is evidence of sub-optimal glycaemic control. After reviewing the patient's ability to change their lifestyle and medication concordance. Following a full discussion with the patient that includes identifying barriers to insulin initiation, e.g. occupational issues, fear of weight gain, fear of hypoglycaemia and fear of injections. | Insulin initiation should be part of a structured educational programme for the patient, and competent health care staff should have sufficient time for initiation and follow-up until glycaemic control is optimized. The decision to start insulin should be made in partnership with the person, and the choice of regimen should cater for individual needs. The person initiating insulin should be trained and competent to do so in line with the national guidelines, and should consult with the physician/diabetologist. Ensure educational materials and support literature are available for the patient starting insulin. Patients requiring insulin prior to pregnancy should be referred to the gynaecologist. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM
text:
### Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM (flowchart)

Steps run from 1 injection (more flexible, lower patient complexity) to 3+ injections (less flexible, high complexity).

Step 1 - Basal insulin (usually with metformin), 1 injection:
  Start: 10 units per day, or 0.1 to 0.2 units per kg per day.
  Adjust: 10% to 15%, or 2 to 4 units, once or twice weekly to reach fasting BG target.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 4 units or 10% to 20%.

If not controlled after fasting BG target is reached (or if dose > 0.5 units per kg per day), treat postprandial glucose excursions with mealtime insulin (consider an initial glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist trial). Two options (2 injections, moderate complexity):

Option A - Add 1 rapid-acting insulin injection before the largest meal:
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose; if A1C <8%, consider decreasing basal insulin by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Option B - Change to premixed insulin twice daily:
  Start: divide current basal dose into 2/3 a.m. and 1/3 p.m., or into 1/2 a.m. and 1/2 p.m.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Step 3 - Add 2 or more rapid-acting insulin injections before the largest meals (basal-bolus, 3+ injections, high complexity):
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose per meal; if A1C < 8%, consider decreasing basal dose by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.

NB: for clients already on a single injectable agent, e.g. basal insulin, consider escalation to any of: 1. combination basal insulin and GLP-1RA therapy; 2. premix (twice daily) insulin; 3. basal-plus insulin therapy (adding one or more prandial doses of insulin to basal insulin). heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 1 Diabetes > Signs and symptoms of type 1 diabetes
text:
### Type 1 diabetes: signs and symptoms by severity (early, severe without loss of consciousness, severe with coma)

All children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes require insulin. Poorly controlled type 1 diabetes increases the risk of stunted growth and diabetes complications, including diabetic ketoacidosis.

| Classification | Sign / symptom | Associated condition / severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early symptoms | Polyuria; polydipsia; polyphagia; weight loss and/or poor weight gain; enuresis/nocturia; fatigue; blurred vision; perineal candidiasis (esp. prepubertal girls); inability and decreasing performance at school | Hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar); dehydration due to fluid loss; cellular energy deficit; catabolism (breakdown of fat/muscle); polyuria (excessive night-time urination); lack of energy utilization; osmotic changes in the eye lens; localized fungal infection due to glucose in urine; general malaise/fatigue/frequent bathroom breaks |
| Severe symptoms (without loss of consciousness) | Polyuria with severe dehydration; polydipsia; fast deep breathing (hyperventilation); presence of fruity (sweet) breath | Uncontrolled hyperglycaemia and significant fluid loss; severe dehydration; compensatory mechanism for metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing); diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): presence of acetone/ketones |
| Severe symptoms (with coma) | Severe hyperglycaemia which may progress to neurological compromise, seizures, and coma | Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 1 Diabetes > Diagnosis of T1DM
text:
### Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes (T1DM)

Three stages, shown as three boxes:
1. Symptoms (loss of weight, polyuria, polydipsia, ...): increased risk of diabetes. Suspect diabetes.
2. Symptoms + glucose criteria: in case of abnormal plasma glucose values, experts suggest getting an HbA1c as a useful baseline. Diabetes is confirmed by: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dl); random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dl); HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Immune-mediated diabetes: presence of autoimmune markers.
3. Immune-mediated diabetes (in tertiary care): presence of autoimmune markers: islet cell autoantibodies and autoantibodies to GAD (GAD65), insulin, the tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2β, and ZnT8.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy for Type 1 Diabetes > Insulin regimens > Insulin dosage regimens
text:
### Insulin dosage regimens for type 1 diabetes: share of total daily dose by meal (basal-bolus, split-mixed, three and two injections)

Basal-bolus regimen (preferred regimen): short acting insulin 15-30 minutes before a meal, or rapid acting insulin with main meals (e.g. breakfast, lunch and main evening meal); intermediate acting insulin before bed. Normally 30-40% of the total daily dose is given at bedtime as intermediate acting insulin; the remaining insulin is given before breakfast, lunch and the evening meal as short acting insulin. Short acting insulin is indicated in the child (especially <5 years of age) with erratic eating habits despite adequate education.

**Option 1: basal-bolus regimen (preferred regimen)**

| Time | Insulin | Share of dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakfast | Short acting insulin | 20% of total daily dose (if able to count carbohydrates: give 1 unit per 15 g) |
| Lunch | Short acting insulin | 20% of total daily dose |
| Supper | Short acting insulin | 20% of total daily dose |
| At night (± 21h00) | Intermediate acting (ideally this ought to be a basal insulin acting over 24 hours) | 40% of total daily dose |

**Option 2 (OR)**

| Time | Insulin | Share of dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakfast | Short acting insulin (30% of morning dose) + intermediate acting (70% of morning dose) | 2/3 of total daily dose |
| Lunch | Short acting insulin (1/3 of evening dose) | 1/3 of total daily dose |
| At night (± 21h00) | Intermediate acting (2/3 of evening dose) | 1/3 of total daily dose |

**Note:** OR three injections daily: a mixture of short and intermediate acting (premixed 70:30) insulin before breakfast; short acting insulin alone before an afternoon snack or main evening meal; intermediate acting insulin before bed (or variations). This requires that the caregiver is aware of three different insulin preparations and can differentiate between them. OR two injections daily: a mixture (premixed combination) of short and intermediate acting insulins before breakfast and the main evening meal. The total daily dose is divided so that 2/3 is given in the morning and 1/3 in the evening; each dose is split between intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin in a 70:30 ratio (pre-mixed). This regimen is less flexible, but easier to give administration instructions for.

Option 1: basal-bolus regimen (preferred regimen)
BreakfastShort acting insulin20% of total daily dose (if able to count carbohydrates: give 1 unit per 15 g)
LunchShort acting insulin20% of total daily dose
SupperShort acting insulin20% of total daily dose
At night (± 21h00)Intermediate acting (ideally this ought to be a basal insulin acting over 24 hours)40% of total daily dose
Option 2 (OR)
BreakfastShort acting insulin (30% of morning dose) + intermediate acting (70% of morning dose)2/3 of total daily dose
LunchShort acting insulin (1/3 of evening dose)1/3 of total daily dose
At night (± 21h00)Intermediate acting (2/3 of evening dose)1/3 of total daily dose
OR three injections daily: a mixture of short and intermediate acting (premixed 70:30) insulin before breakfast; short acting insulin alone before an afternoon snack or main evening meal; intermediate acting insulin before bed (or variations). This requires that the caregiver is aware of three different insulin preparations and can differentiate between them. OR two injections daily: a mixture (premixed combination) of short and intermediate acting insulins before breakfast and the main evening meal. The total daily dose is divided so that 2/3 is given in the morning and 1/3 in the evening; each dose is split between intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin in a 70:30 ratio (pre-mixed). This regimen is less flexible, but easier to give administration instructions for.

text:
### Management of diabetic emergencies (DKA and HHS): diagnosis, evaluation, monitoring, resolution, transition to SC insulin, alternative SC insulin protocol and formulas

| Topic | Guidance |
| --- | --- |
| Introduction | Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia without ketoacidosis. |
| Diagnosis (DKA & HHS) | Based on clinical evaluation and immediate bedside investigations. Features include polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity odor, confusion, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration. |
| Diabetic ketoacidosis criteria | Hyperglycemia: BG >13.9 mmol/L. Euglycemia <250 mg/dl (pregnancy, SGLT2 use). Ketonuria or ketonemia (>3 mmol/L): highly positive. Acidosis: pH <7.3, low HCO3- (printed ':<10 ≤ 15 mEq/L'). Anion gap: >12 (see formula). |
| Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state criteria | Severe hyperglycemia: BG (printed '>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3 mmol/L'). Hyperosmolality: effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula). Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma. |
| Evaluation | Vital signs, volume status (decreased skin turgor, dry axillae and oral mucosa, low JVP, tachycardia and hypotension), mental status. Immediately: serum blood glucose, urine ketones. Additional testing: FBC, electrolytes, FT, ABG. Evaluate for precipitating causes: septic screen (urinalysis, blood cultures), cardiac enzymes, ECG, CXR. Pregnancy test if indicated. |
| Monitoring | BG hourly. Urinary ketones and serum pH for DKA, and serum osmolality for HHS, 4-hourly. Electrolytes, primarily Na+ and K+, 4-hourly. Mental status: expect improvement with treatment if DKA or HHS are the causes; consider further evaluation if not improving. Input/output, hydration status; vital signs hourly. |
| Criteria for resolution: DKA | BG < 15 mmol/L + 2 or more of: HCO3- ≥ 15 mEq/L; pH > 7.3; anion gap ≤ 12 mEq/L. Negative urine ketones if the above are not available (confirm with repeat in 1-2 hrs). |
| Criteria for resolution: HHS | BG < [value missing in source]; improved mental status; effective osmolality ≤ 315 mOsm/kg. |
| Transition to long-acting insulin | Continue continuous IV for 1-2 hrs after long-acting insulin is started. 0.4-0.6 u/kg for insulin-naive patients. NPH/regular: based on inpatient DM protocol. Hold regular insulin if patient is not eating. May resume home regimen if previously on insulin. |
| Alternative subcutaneous insulin protocol | This regimen is not well validated and is modified from other protocols; continuous IV is preferred as standard of care when available. If continuous infusion is not available, for mild/moderate DKA: initial IV bolus 0.1 IU/kg given intravenously; maintenance 0.1 IU/kg subcutaneous every 1-2 hours (start immediately following the bolus). When BG <250 mg/dL, reduce dose by 50%. Continue until resolution of DKA or HHS. |
| Useful formulas | Calculated anion gap (>12 is elevated) = [Na+] − [Cl- + HCO3-]. Effective serum osmolality = 2x[Na+K] + urea + glucose (usually <330 mosmol/kg in DKA and > 350 mosmol/kg in HHS). Corrected serum sodium = [Na+] + 1.6 x [glucose (mg/dL) − 100]/100. Free water deficit = 0.6 x weight (kg) x [(Na+/140) − 1]. |

| Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state criteria | Severe hyperglycemia: BG (printed '>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3 mmol/L'). Hyperosmolality: effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula). Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma. |

| Alternative subcutaneous insulin protocol | This regimen is not well validated and is modified from other protocols; continuous IV is preferred as standard of care when available. Management of diabetic emergencies (DKA and HHS): diagnosis, evaluation, monitoring, resolution, transition to SC insulin, alternative SC insulin protocol and formulas
TopicGuidance
IntroductionDiabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia without ketoacidosis.
Diagnosis (DKA & HHS)Based on clinical evaluation and immediate bedside investigations. Features include polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity odor, confusion, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration.
Diabetic ketoacidosis criteriaHyperglycemia: BG >13.9 mmol/L. Euglycemia <250 mg/dl (pregnancy, SGLT2 use). Ketonuria or ketonemia (>3 mmol/L): highly positive. Acidosis: pH <7.3, low HCO3- (printed ':<10 ≤ 15 mEq/L'). Anion gap: >12 (see formula).
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state criteriaSevere hyperglycemia: BG (printed '>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3 mmol/L'). Hyperosmolality: effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula). Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma.
EvaluationVital signs, volume status (decreased skin turgor, dry axillae and oral mucosa, low JVP, tachycardia and hypotension), mental status. Immediately: serum blood glucose, urine ketones. Additional testing: FBC, electrolytes, FT, ABG. Evaluate for precipitating causes: septic screen (urinalysis, blood cultures), cardiac enzymes, ECG, CXR. Pregnancy test if indicated.
MonitoringBG hourly. Urinary ketones and serum pH for DKA, and serum osmolality for HHS, 4-hourly. Electrolytes, primarily Na+ and K+, 4-hourly. Mental status: expect improvement with treatment if DKA or HHS are the causes; consider further evaluation if not improving. Input/output, hydration status; vital signs hourly.
Criteria for resolution: DKABG < 15 mmol/L + 2 or more of: HCO3- ≥ 15 mEq/L; pH > 7.3; anion gap ≤ 12 mEq/L. Negative urine ketones if the above are not available (confirm with repeat in 1-2 hrs).
Criteria for resolution: HHSBG < [value missing in source]; improved mental status; effective osmolality ≤ 315 mOsm/kg.
Transition to long-acting insulinContinue continuous IV for 1-2 hrs after long-acting insulin is started. 0.4-0.6 u/kg for insulin-naive patients. NPH/regular: based on inpatient DM protocol. Hold regular insulin if patient is not eating. May resume home regimen if previously on insulin.
Alternative subcutaneous insulin protocolThis regimen is not well validated and is modified from other protocols; continuous IV is preferred as standard of care when available. If continuous infusion is not available, for mild/moderate DKA: initial IV bolus 0.1 IU/kg given intravenously; maintenance 0.1 IU/kg subcutaneous every 1-2 hours (start immediately following the bolus). When BG <250 mg/dL, reduce dose by 50%. Continue until resolution of DKA or HHS.
Useful formulasCalculated anion gap (>12 is elevated) = [Na+] − [Cl- + HCO3-]. Effective serum osmolality = 2x[Na+K] + urea + glucose (usually <330 mosmol/kg in DKA and > 350 mosmol/kg in HHS). Corrected serum sodium = [Na+] + 1.6 x [glucose (mg/dL) − 100]/100. Free water deficit = 0.6 x weight (kg) x [(Na+/140) − 1].

### 01 Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): diagnostic criteria (all 3 required) and severity

| Criterion | Threshold | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blood glucose | >11 mmol/L (or known DM) | Can occur at lower levels in pregnancy |
| Venous pH / HCO3- | pH <7.3 OR HCO3- <15 mmol/L | VBG preferred over ABG |
| Ketonaemia | ≥3 mmol/L (serum) | Ketonuria ≥2+ if no POC ketone meter |
| Severity | Mild: pH 7.25-7.30. Moderate: pH 7.00-7.24. Severe: pH <7.00 | Severe cases need ICU-level care |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 02 Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) criteria
text:
### 02 Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS): diagnostic criteria (all 3 required) and osmolality target

| Criterion | Threshold | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blood glucose | >30 mmol/L | Often 50-80 mmol/L at presentation |
| Serum osmolality | ≥320 mOsm/kg | Formula: 2(Na+ + K+) + glucose |
| Acidosis / ketones | Absent / mild: pH >7.3, HCO3- >15 | Mixed DKA/HHS can occur |
| Osmolality target | Reduce by 3-8 mOsm/kg/hr | Do not fall below 310 in first 24 hrs |

**Note:** WARNING: Do NOT delay treatment to await full investigation results. Start fluids and check K+ immediately. Insulin is CONTRAINDICATED if K+ <3.5 mmol/L.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 03 IV fluid resuscitation
text:
### 03 IV fluid resuscitation in DKA and HHS: regimen and rate by time

Use 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) as first-line. Switch to 0.45% NaCl in HHS once glucose <20 mmol/L and osmolality falling. Add 5% dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L (DKA) or <15 mmol/L (HHS) to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia.

| Time | DKA regimen | HHS regimen | Rate guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0-60 min | 0.9% NaCl: 1 L over 30-60 min. If SBP <90: 500 ml bolus, repeat once | 0.9% NaCl: 1 L over 60 min. Slower if elderly/cardiac risk | ~15-20 ml/kg |
| 1-4 hr | 0.9% NaCl: 500 ml/hr x2 hrs, then 250 ml/hr | 0.9% NaCl: 500 ml/hr (adjust to deficit) | 250-500 ml/hr |
| 4-12 hr | 0.9% NaCl 125-250 ml/hr; switch to 0.45% NaCl if corrected Na+ rising | 0.45% NaCl 250 ml/hr once osmolality falling; correct deficit over 48 hrs | 125-250 ml/hr |
| BGL <14 (DKA) / <15 (HHS) | Switch to 0.9% NaCl + 5% dextrose OR 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose. Continue insulin: use dextrose to maintain target glucose range. | 150 ml/hr |  |

**Note:** WARNING: HHS: total deficit can be 8-15 litres. Correct over 48-72 hours. Rapid correction risks cerebral oedema and cardiac failure. Reassess every 2 hours. Target osmolality reduction 3-8 mOsm/kg/hr.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 06 Bicarbonate (DKA only, restricted use)
text:
### 06 Bicarbonate in DKA (restricted use): indication and regimen

WARNING: Do NOT routinely give bicarbonate in DKA: associated with paradoxical CNS acidosis, hypokalaemia, and worsened cerebral oedema.

| Indication | Regimen |
| --- | --- |
| pH <6.9 OR life-threatening hyperkalaemia (K+ >6.5 with ECG changes) | 100 mmol (100 ml of 8.4%) NaHCO3 IV over 30 minutes. Add 20 mmol KCl to each infusion. Repeat VBG after 60 min; maximum 2 doses. Not recommended in HHS. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 05 Insulin protocol
text:
### 05 Insulin protocol: DKA insulin infusion vs HHS insulin protocol

| DKA: insulin infusion | HHS: insulin protocol |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Bolus (only if K+ ≥3.5): 0.1 unit/kg soluble (regular) insulin IV stat. 2. Continuous infusion: 0.1 unit/kg/hr soluble insulin IV. Dilute 50 units in 50 ml 0.9% NaCl (1 unit/ml) via syringe pump. If no pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml). 3. When glucose <14 mmol/L: reduce to 0.05 unit/kg/hr + add 5% dextrose to fluids. Target BGL 10-14 mmol/L until ketones clear / pH >7.3. | Step 1: fluids only for the first 1-2 hours, NO insulin. Glucose will fall with fluids alone; early insulin causes rapid osmolality drop and cerebral oedema. Step 2: start insulin only when glucose is NOT falling >5 mmol/L/hr with fluids alone AND adequate fluid resuscitation is underway. Start at 0.05 unit/kg/hr (lower than DKA). Step 3: target glucose reduction 3-4 mmol/L/hr. Target BGL 10-15 mmol/L. NEVER drop >5 mmol/L/hr. |

**Note:** WARNING: Avoid SC insulin during IV fluid resuscitation: poor absorption due to vasoconstriction and dehydration. Do not stop insulin to treat hypoglycaemia: reduce rate and add dextrose.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 04 Potassium replacement protocol
text:
### 04 Potassium replacement protocol in DKA/HHS: action, KCl per litre and rate by serum K+

| Serum K+ (mmol/L) | Action | KCl per litre fluid | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <3.5 | HOLD INSULIN: replace K+ urgently first. Recheck K+ in 1 hour before restarting insulin. | 40 mmol KCl (central line only for >20 mmol/hr) | Replace until K+ ≥3.5 |
| 3.5-5.5 | Normal: proceed with insulin. Monitor every 2 hours. | 20-40 mmol KCl per litre | 10-20 mmol/hr |
| >5.5 | Hold K+ supplementation. Recheck in 2 hours. | No KCl: monitor for hyperkalaemia | 10-20 mmol/hr |

**Note:** Potassium safety rules: NEVER give undiluted KCl IV (fatal if bolused). Rates >20 mmol/hr require cardiac monitoring and central venous access. Initial K+ may appear high/normal despite total body depletion: watch closely as insulin drives K+ intracellularly. Hypokalaemia is the leading cause of preventable death in DKA.

text:
### 07 Monitoring schedule for DKA/HHS, and corrected sodium in hyperglycaemia

| Frequency | Parameter |
| --- | --- |
| Every 1 hour | Capillary blood glucose, fluid balance (in/out), HR, BP, SpO2, RR |
| Every 2 hours | Serum K+, Na+, urea; venous blood gas; blood or urine ketones |
| Every 4 hours | Full U&E + creatinine; reassess fluid plan; neurological status |
| Continuous | ECG if K+ abnormal or arrhythmia present |
| Every 1-2 hr (HHS) | GCS: declining = cerebral oedema: STOP fluids and escalate |
| Urinary output | Target >0.5 ml/kg/hr. Catheterise if anuric or GCS <13 |

**Note:** Corrected sodium in hyperglycaemia: measured Na+ is falsely low in hyperglycaemia. Add 1.6 mmol/L to measured Na+ for every 5.5 mmol/L glucose above 5.5 mmol/L. If corrected Na+ is rising despite resuscitation, switch to 0.45% NaCl. Persistent hypernatraemia in HHS suggests under-resuscitation.

text:
### 08 Resolution criteria for DKA and HHS, and 3-step transition to subcutaneous insulin

**Resolution criteria (ALL required)**

| Item | Criteria / action |
| --- | --- |
| DKA resolution | Blood glucose <14 mmol/L; venous pH >7.3; HCO3- >15 mmol/L; ketonaemia <0.6 mmol/L (or ketonuria <1+); patient able to eat and drink. |
| HHS resolution | Serum osmolality <310 mOsm/kg; blood glucose <15 mmol/L; clinically well, normal GCS; patient eating and drinking; no further vomiting. |

**Transition to subcutaneous insulin: 3-step protocol**

| Item | Criteria / action |
| --- | --- |
| Step 1 | Give SC insulin dose at mealtime. Ensure patient has eaten before injecting. |
| Step 2 | Continue IV insulin infusion for at least 30-60 minutes AFTER SC injection to avoid gap. |
| Step 3 | Known DM: resume pre-admission regimen. New DM: start basal-bolus 0.5 unit/kg/day (50% basal, 50% bolus divided over 3 meals). |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Complications to anticipate and manage
text:
### DKA/HHS complications to anticipate: recognition and management, and when to escalate

| Complication | Recognition | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cerebral oedema | Declining GCS, headache, bradycardia after initial improvement | Reduce fluids; mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV; urgent transfer to higher level |
| Hypokalaemia | Commonest preventable death. ECG: U waves, ST depression, QT prolongation | Check K+ every 2 hrs, replace aggressively per protocol (section 04) |
| Hypoglycaemia | Glucose falling too rapidly or <4 mmol/L | Add dextrose to fluids; NEVER stop insulin: reduce rate instead |
| Hyperchloraemic acidosis | Non-anion gap acidosis despite DKA treatment, large NS volumes given | Switch to balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) if available; reduce NS |
| Thromboembolism (HHS) | High risk in HHS: may be clinically silent | LMWH prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (no contraindication). TED stockings |
| Pulmonary oedema | Crackles on auscultation, SpO2 falling, worsening dyspnoea | Reduce fluid rate; furosemide if fluid overloaded; CXR; oxygen |
| Acute kidney injury | Urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hr persisting after resuscitation | Ensure adequate fluids; avoid nephrotoxins; urgent nephrology review if severe |
| Infection / sepsis | Fever, leukocytosis, clinical signs of source | Empirical antibiotics: co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone; cultures before antibiotics; check HIV |

**Note:** WARNING: ESCALATE TO HIGHER LEVEL OF CARE if GCS <13, pH <7.0, K+ <2.5 or >7.0, SBP <80 not responding to fluids, declining despite 4 hours of treatment, suspected cerebral oedema, pregnancy with DKA, or need for ICU monitoring. Contact Mbabane Government Hospital or Raleigh Fitkin Memorial Hospital referral pathway.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for DKA
text:
### Algorithm for DKA (flowchart: assessment, resuscitation, IV therapy, insulin, monitoring, cerebral oedema)

Immediate assessment:
- Clinical history: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, enuresis, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, fatigue, confusion, level of consciousness.
- Clinical signs: dehydration; deep sighing respiration (Kussmaul); smell of ketones; lethargy/drowsiness.
- Biochemical features & investigations: ketones in urine; blood glucose; acidaemia (vpH < 7.3, HCO3 <15 mmol/L); urea, electrolytes; other investigations as indicated.
Diagnosis confirmed: diabetic ketoacidosis. Contact senior staff.

Then by clinical state:
A. Shock (reduced peripheral pulses), reduced conscious level/coma: resuscitation: airway ± NG tube; breathing (100% oxygen); circulation: 0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h, repeat until circulation is restored (see CE management). Then IV therapy (as B).
B. Dehydration >5%, not in shock, acidotic (hyperventilation), vomiting: IV therapy: saline 0.9% 10 ml/kg over 1 h, may repeat; calculate fluid requirements; correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours; ECG for abnormal T-waves; add KCl 40 mmol per litre of fluid.
C. Minimal dehydration, tolerating oral fluid: therapy: start with SC insulin; continue oral hydration. If no improvement: IV therapy (as B).

After IV therapy: continuous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, starting 1 hour after fluids initiated.

Critical observations: hourly blood glucose; hourly fluid input & output; neurological status at least hourly; electrolytes 2-hourly after starting IV fluid therapy; monitor ECG for T-wave changes.

Then:
- Acidosis not improving: re-evaluate IV fluid calculations, insulin delivery system & dose, need for additional resuscitation; consider sepsis.
- Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL): IV therapy: change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5%-12.5%) to prevent hypoglycaemia; adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium. When improved (clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids): transition to SC insulin: start SC insulin, then stop IV insulin after an appropriate interval.
- Neurological deterioration: warning signs: severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs. Exclude hypoglycaemia; is it cerebral oedema? CE (cerebral oedema) management: give mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline; adjust IV fluids to maintain normal BP but avoid over-hydration; call senior staff; move to ICU; consider cranial imaging only after the patient is stabilized.

A. Shock (reduced peripheral pulses), reduced conscious level/coma: resuscitation: airway ± NG tube; breathing (100% oxygen); circulation: 0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h, repeat until circulation is restored (see CE management). Then IV therapy (as B).
B. Dehydration >5%, not in shock, acidotic (hyperventilation), vomiting: IV therapy: saline 0.9% 10 ml/kg over 1 h, may repeat; calculate fluid requirements; correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours; ECG for abnormal T-waves; add KCl 40 mmol per litre of fluid.
C. Minimal dehydration, tolerating oral fluid: therapy: start with SC insulin; continue oral hydration. If no improvement: IV therapy (as B).

After IV therapy: continuous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, starting 1 hour after fluids initiated.

Critical observations: hourly blood glucose; hourly fluid input & output; neurological status at least hourly; electrolytes 2-hourly after starting IV fluid therapy; monitor ECG for T-wave changes.

Then:
- Acidosis not improving: re-evaluate IV fluid calculations, insulin delivery system & dose, need for additional resuscitation; consider sepsis.
- Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL): IV therapy: change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5%-12.5%) to prevent hypoglycaemia; adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium. When improved (clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids): transition to SC insulin: start SC insulin, then stop IV insulin after an appropriate interval.
- Neurological deterioration: warning signs: severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs. Exclude hypoglycaemia; is it cerebral oedema? CE (cerebral oedema) management: give mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline; adjust IV fluids to maintain normal BP but avoid over-hydration; call senior staff; move to ICU; consider cranial imaging only after the patient is stabilized.

text:
### Management of hypoglycaemia by level (mild, moderate, severe): glucose thresholds and actions

| Level | Blood glucose | Description | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Level 1 (mild): hypoglycaemia alert | ≤ 3.9 mmol/L but ≥ 3.0 mmol/L | Requires treatment with fast-acting carbohydrate. Patient alert and able to eat. | Treat with oral glucose. Give a sugary snack and recheck blood glucose in 15 min. If blood glucose remains ≤ 3.9 mmol/L, repeat the previous step. Give a carbohydrate meal when blood glucose is ≥ 5.0 mmol/L. |
| Level 2 (moderate): clinically significant hypoglycaemia | < 3.0 mmol/L | Indicates serious, clinically significant hypoglycaemia. Patient may be alert or may have reduced consciousness. | Treat with IV glucose. Give 10 ml 50% glucose IV and recheck blood glucose in 2 min. If blood glucose remains <5 mmol/L, repeat the previous step. Give an infusion of 10% glucose IV if more than 2 doses of IV glucose are required. Give a carbohydrate meal when blood glucose is ≥ 5.0 mmol/L and the patient is alert and able to eat. Observe for 4 hrs, checking blood glucose every 1 hr. |
| Level 3 (severe) | No specific value | Associated with severe cognitive impairment requiring external help for recovery. Patient has reduced consciousness. | Treat as for level 2 hypoglycaemia. Likely to need hospital admission. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Hypoglycemia > Clinical presentation
text:
### Hypoglycaemia clinical presentation: adrenergic (early) vs neuroglycopenic (late) symptoms

Hypoglycaemia is a medical emergency, characterized by blood glucose <4 mmol/L. Some patients may have symptoms at higher levels; individualize care.

| Adrenergic (early) symptoms | Neuroglycopenic (late) symptoms |
| --- | --- |
| Severe hunger; cold, clammy skin; profuse sweating; palpitations; tremors; weakness; headache | Irritability; confusion; disorientation; seizures; coma; sudden collapse (common in type 1 DM or in hypoglycaemia unawareness) |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Glycemic Control in Non-Critical Hospitalized Adult Patients Protocols > Total daily insulin (TDI) starting dose by patient type
text:
### Total daily insulin (TDI) starting dose by patient type (non-critical hospitalized adults)

Inpatient hyperglycaemia is a random blood glucose ≥ 7.8 mmol/L in a non-critical hospitalized patient. Admission HbA1c is recommended for all patients with diabetes or hyperglycaemia (>7.8 mmol/L) if not done in the last 3 months. A basal-bolus + correction approach is recommended; sole reliance on sliding scale insulin (SSI) is strongly discouraged (ADA & SEMDSA).

| Patient type | Clinical characteristics | Insulin sensitivity | Recommended TDI starting dose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Insulin-naive, normal weight | Newly diagnosed; BMI 18-30; eating reliably; normal renal function | Normal sensitivity | 0.3-0.4 units/kg/day |
| Insulin-sensitive / high risk for hypoglycaemia | Elderly (>65); renal/hepatic impairment; frail; underweight; NPO | High sensitivity | 0.15-0.2 units/kg/day (basal-only: 0.1-0.2). Reduce PM NPH by 20-30% if nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk |
| Obese / overweight type 2 diabetes | BMI >30; known insulin resistance | Insulin-resistant | 0.5-0.6 units/kg/day |
| Marked insulin resistance | Chronic steroids; severe infection/sepsis; systemic inflammation; high-dose steroids; pregnancy; T2DM poor control | Very insulin-resistant | 0.7-1.0 units/kg/day |
| Previously on insulin (well-controlled) | On basal-bolus or premix; admission not related to hyperglycaemia | Use previous insulin need | 70-100% of home TDI depending on oral intake |
| Previously on insulin (poor control) | High HbA1c (>9%); persistent hyperglycaemia | Often insulin-resistant | 0.5-0.6 units/kg/day (or increase previous TDI by 10-20% per glucose profile) |

text:
### Capillary blood glucose (CBG) insulin correction dose scale: units to add by CBG reading and insulin sensitivity

| CBG reading | Pre-meal dose: sensitive (BMI <25 or TDI <50 units/d) | Pre-meal dose: average (BMI 25-30 or TDI 50-90 units/d) | Pre-meal dose: resistant (BMI >30 or TDI >90 units/d) | Bedtime dose (eating patients only) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| < 3.9 mmol/L | Follow hypoglycaemia protocol | Follow hypoglycaemia protocol | Follow hypoglycaemia protocol | Follow hypoglycaemia protocol |
| 3.9 - 8.3 mmol/L | Give scheduled insulin only: no correction dose required | Give scheduled insulin only: no correction dose required | Give scheduled insulin only: no correction dose required | Give scheduled insulin only: no correction dose required |
| 8.4 - 11.1 mmol/L | 1 unit | 2 units | 3 units | 0 units |
| 11.2 - 13.9 mmol/L | 2 units | 4 units | 6 units | 1 unit |
| 14.0 - 16.7 mmol/L | 3 units | 6 units | 9 units | 2 units |
| 16.8 - 19.4 mmol/L | 4 units | 8 units | 12 units | 3 units |
| 19.5 - 22.2 mmol/L | 5 units + CALL | 10 units + CALL | 15 units + CALL | 3 units + CALL |
| > 22.2 mmol/L | 6 units + CALL | 12 units + CALL | 18 units + CALL | 3 units + CALL |

Key notes: correction doses are based on fasting or pre-meal BG readings only. The correction dose is ADDED to the scheduled (basal-bolus) insulin dose. Bedtime correction doses apply to eating patients only; omit for NPO patients; bedtime correction doses should be REDUCED by 50%. '+ CALL' = notify the prescriber immediately for clinical review. NPO patients: consider IV fluids and TPN; consult endocrinologist; administer SC insulin only as directed; reduce bolus insulin and use the level 1 correction scale; reassess TDI daily. If hypoglycaemia occurs or is recurrent, step DOWN one sensitivity level (resistant to average to sensitive). Reassess TDI and correction scale level daily based on glucose trends and clinical status. Adapted from Umpierrez et al. & Magaji et al. TDI = total daily insulin; NPO = nil per os; SC = subcutaneous; TPN = total parenteral nutrition.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Glycemic Control in Non-Critical Hospitalized Adult Patients Protocols > Insulin subcutaneous: basal, bolus and correction (sliding scale) order protocol
text:
### Subcutaneous insulin order protocol (basal, bolus and correction) for adult non-ICU patients who are NPO, on TPN, eating or tube-fed

Sliding scale insulin is designed to be given occasionally in addition to the scheduled bolus dose to correct unexpected hyperglycaemia; it should not be given routinely OR BY ITSELF. Add up all insulin over 24 hours from all components of the pre-admission regimen and choose the dose scale according to 24-hour insulin use; consider starting at low dose for patients at high risk of hypoglycaemia (renal dysfunction, hypoglycaemia unawareness, insulin-naive, elderly). If correction insulin is given frequently, reassess the basal and nutritional doses. During initiation, the next day's basal dose can be increased by carefully adding 50% of the previous day's correction doses (excluding the nutritional component).

| Section | Instruction |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | For adult patients who are NPO\*, on TPN\*\*, eating meals, or on bolus or continuous tube feedings. Not used for ICU patients, DKA, or hyperosmolar state. Initiate the protocol for adult patients with known diabetes mellitus and anyone with two or more random (e.g., 6 hours apart) blood glucose readings > 10 mmol/l (order HbA1c if none obtained). |
| Goal of therapy | To minimize the need for correction insulin doses (sliding scale) and to provide insulin as regularly scheduled basal and bolus insulin for more efficient control of blood glucose. To maintain capillary blood glucose (CBG) at 7.8-10.0 mmol/L. |
| Monitoring | Measure CBG: eating patients: before meals and at bedtime; bolus tube-feeding patients: before each feeding; NPO or continuous tube-feeding patients: every 4 hours (rapid insulin) or every 6 hours (regular insulin). In case of high morning blood sugar, measure CBG at 3:00 a.m. to distinguish between Somogyi effect and dawn phenomenon. |
| Medications | Discontinue all previous antihyperglycemic agents (injection/oral): yes/no; if yes, continue to calculate the insulin dose. Calculate the initial total daily insulin (TDI) per day: 0.25 units per kg: chronic kidney disease not on dialysis; 0.3 units per kg: underweight (BMI < 18.5), older age (≥65 years), haemodialysis; 0.4 units per kg: normal weight (BMI 18.5-24.9); 0.5 units per kg: overweight (BMI 25.0-29.9); ≥ 0.6 units per kg: obese (BMI ≥30), glucocorticoids, insulin resistance. |
| Basal insulin (longer acting) | Order 50% of the TDI. Should be given even if NPO\*. Reduce dose by 25% if NPO\*/poor intake/glycaemia well controlled. ___ units subcutaneous at ___ (Q24 or Q12 hours). |
| Bolus insulin (shorter acting) | Order 50% of the TDI. HOLD if NPO\*, TPN\*\*, low oral intake. Divided equally before each meal/bolus feed. If continuous feed: every 4 hours (rapid insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin). Insulin REGULAR: ___ units SC 30 minutes BEFORE each meal/bolus feed, or every 6 hours if continuous feed. |
| Correction / sliding scale (shorter acting) | SHOULD be ordered and given even if NPO\*. Eating patients: before meals and at bedtime (prefer rapid acting insulin); insulin REGULAR SC 30 minutes before meals. Bolus feed patients: before each feeding. TPN\*\*, NPO\* or continuous tube feeding: every 4 hours (rapid acting insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin). |

text:
### Subcutaneous insulin order protocol (basal, bolus and correction) for adult non-ICU patients who are NPO, on TPN, eating or tube-fed

Sliding scale insulin is designed to be given occasionally in addition to the scheduled bolus dose to correct unexpected hyperglycaemia; it should not be given routinely OR BY ITSELF. Add up all insulin over 24 hours from all components of the pre-admission regimen and choose the dose scale according to 24-hour insulin use; consider starting at low dose for patients at high risk of hypoglycaemia (renal dysfunction, hypoglycaemia unawareness, insulin-naive, elderly). If correction insulin is given frequently, reassess the basal and nutritional doses. During initiation, the next day's basal dose can be increased by carefully adding 50% of the previous day's correction doses (excluding the nutritional component).

text:
### Chronic microvascular complications of diabetes (nephropathy, eye disease, neuropathy): who to screen, how, management and referral criteria

| Complication | Who should be screened | Screening/detection method | Treatment/management principles | Urgent referral/action criteria |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Diabetes nephropathy | Type 1 diabetes: duration > 5 years. Type 2 diabetes: at diagnosis. | Yearly check for proteinuria (reagent strips); if positive, exclude/treat UTIs, then refer if persistent. Yearly check for microalbuminuria (reagent strips or ACR). Measure serum creatinine bi-annually. | Optimize glycaemic control (with caution in advanced disease). Aggressive BP control (<125/75 mmHg). Use ACEI or ARBs as first-line (contraindicated in pregnancy). Stop tobacco use. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides). Metformin should not be used if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2. | Persistent microalbuminuria. Inability to optimize blood pressure. Intolerance of ACEI/ARBs or >30% increase in creatinine within 3 months. Consider other causes if: extreme proteinuria (>6 g/day), persistent haematuria, rapidly falling eGFR, low eGFR with low/no proteinuria, diabetes <5 years. |
| Diabetes eye disease (retinopathy & cataracts) | Type 2 diabetes: at presentation. Type 1 diabetes: >5 years duration (or at presentation if uncontrolled). | Full eye examination including visual acuity and fundoscopy (preferably dilated) at initial contact; refer if no capacity. Repeat examinations annually, or more frequently if retinopathy is progressing. Women planning pregnancy and during the first trimester require a comprehensive exam. Type 1 pregnant women: fundoscopy every trimester. | Intensify management of blood pressure, glycaemia, and lipids. Stop smoking. Patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy should avoid weight-bearing exercises and require guided exercises. | Sudden deterioration of vision. 'Floater' sensation reported by patient. Fundoscopy findings of dot or blot haemorrhages 1 disc-width away from the macula. Cataract present. Proliferative or exudative retinopathy. |
| Diabetes neuropathy (motor, sensory, autonomic) | Not specified as a screening criterion, but assessment is part of clinical care. | Detailed history (numbness, tingling, pain). Examination of the feet: test sensation using 10 g monofilament, 128 Hz tuning fork, or cotton wool. Lying-and-standing BP and pulse rate to check for postural hypotension. | Improve glycaemic control. Exclude or treat other contributory factors (e.g., alcohol, B12 deficiency, smoking, HIV). Symptomatic treatment (see peripheral neuropathy guidelines). | Referral to secondary and/or tertiary centre once symptomatic peripheral neuropathy is diagnosed. |

text:
### Diabetes in pregnancy classification (flowchart)

Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is any degree of onset or first recognized during pregnancy impaired glucose tolerance. Glucose values fall into the diagnostic ranges of either impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or diabetes (DM).

Diabetes in pregnancy divides into:
- Pre-existing diabetes: type 1 or type 2.
- [Hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy] (box printed 'Preexisting Diabetes'): either pre-existing diabetes or true GDM (usually at 24-28 weeks).

text:
### Diabetes in pregnancy vs gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): definition, onset, diagnostic criteria, management and postpartum follow-up

| Feature | Diabetes in pregnancy | Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Pregnancy in a woman known to have pre-existing diabetes (type 1 or type 2), or hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy that meets WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state | Hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy (usually in 2nd or 3rd trimester) that does not meet WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state |
| Timing of onset | May occur at any time, including the 1st trimester | Typically develops in the 2nd or 3rd trimester |
| Underlying type | Usually type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus | Pregnancy-induced glucose intolerance |
| Diagnostic criteria (WHO / IADPSG) | Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥ 7.0 mmol/L OR 2-hour OGTT (75 g glucose) ≥ 11.1 mmol/L OR random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms | Any one of the following (on 75 g OGTT): fasting ≥ 5.1 mmol/L; 1-hour ≥ 10.0 mmol/L; 2-hour ≥ 8.5 mmol/L |
| Management focus | (not stated; see postpartum row for pre-existing diabetes care) | Dietary modification and physical activity. Monitor blood glucose regularly and start metformin if glycaemic control is not reached. Insulin therapy if lifestyle and metformin measures fail. Postpartum screening for type 2 DM. |
| Postpartum follow-up | Optimize pre-existing diabetes control before and during pregnancy. Frequent glucose monitoring. Adjust insulin regimen as needed. Fetal growth and anomaly surveillance. | Reassess glycaemic status 6-12 weeks postpartum; repeat OGTT every year to detect type 2 DM. |
