text:
### Gestational diabetes (GDM): screening, risk factors, management, glycaemic goals, complications and preconception plan

**Screening**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Universal screening (every pregnant woman) is recommended. If the woman has more than one risk factor, do an RBS/FBS at first contact. Screening should be done at 24-28 weeks (or at first contact if the patient presents late). Perform a 75 g OGTT: administer 75 g of glucose orally after an 8-hr overnight fast and measure blood glucose after 1 hour and 2 hours (1 standard level teaspoon = 5 g). | (same as left) |

**Risk factors for GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk factors | Previous GDM; maternal age > 35 years; family history of diabetes (first-degree relative); obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2); previous macrosomia (birthweight > 4000 g); polycystic ovary syndrome; iatrogenic: glucocorticoids and antipsychotic medication; hypertension. | Intermediate hyperglycaemia or impaired glucose tolerance: HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose. HbA1c >6.5%: diagnosis of pre-existing diabetes. Note: symptoms may be non-specific. |

**Management of GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifestyle modification | Exercise 30-60 min moderate intensity. Diet: regular meal plan; 3 moderate-sized meals, 4 snacks; low sugar. Pharmacotherapy: see the GDM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule. | (same as left) |
| Glycaemic goal | Fasting and pre-prandial blood glucose <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Two-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Check HbA1c every 4-6 weeks; goal below 6.5%. | (same as left) |

**Complications**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short term | Maternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding. | Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome. |
| Long term | Maternal-neonatal: recurrence of GDM; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; ischaemic heart disease; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; dyslipidaemia; chronic kidney disease; metabolic syndrome; hyperinsulinaemia. | Fetal: childhood obesity; excess abdominal adiposity; higher blood pressure; possible earlier-onset cardiovascular disease; possible attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; autism spectrum disorder. |

**Preconception plan**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prior to pregnancy | Optimize modifiable risk factors (e.g. BMI, diet, physical activity). Screen glycaemia in high-risk women. For pre-existing DM: maintain HbA1c below 6% with appropriate drugs (insulin and metformin). Screen for complications. | (same as left) |
| During pregnancy | Healthy diet and regular exercise unless there are obstetric contraindications. Possible personalized gestational weight gain. High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception screening positive). Follow the protocol for all at 24-28 weeks according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria. Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if sugars are well controlled; if poorly controlled, consult a specialist on timing of delivery. Consider steroids for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated. If steroids are given at any point in pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control; insulin therapy is advised. Aim for blood glucose 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery. Anticipate maternal and fetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions. | (same as left) |
| Postpartum | Early postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status. Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification. Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring. | (same as left) |

Screening should be done at 24-28 weeks (or at first contact if the patient presents late). Perform a 75 g OGTT: administer 75 g of glucose orally after an 8-hr overnight fast and measure blood glucose after 1 hour and 2 hours (1 standard level teaspoon = 5 g). | (same as left) |

**Risk factors for GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk factors | Previous GDM; maternal age > 35 years; family history of diabetes (first-degree relative); obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2); previous macrosomia (birthweight > 4000 g); polycystic ovary syndrome; iatrogenic: glucocorticoids and antipsychotic medication; hypertension. | Intermediate hyperglycaemia or impaired glucose tolerance: HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose. HbA1c >6.5%: diagnosis of pre-existing diabetes. Note: symptoms may be non-specific. |

**Management of GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifestyle modification | Exercise 30-60 min moderate intensity. Diet: regular meal plan; 3 moderate-sized meals, 4 snacks; low sugar. Pharmacotherapy: see the GDM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule. | (same as left) |
| Glycaemic goal | Fasting and pre-prandial blood glucose <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Two-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Check HbA1c every 4-6 weeks; goal below 6.5%. | (same as left) |

**Complications**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short term | Maternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding. | Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome. |
| Long term | Maternal-neonatal: recurrence of GDM; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; ischaemic heart disease; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; dyslipidaemia; chronic kidney disease; metabolic syndrome; hyperinsulinaemia. | Fetal: childhood obesity; excess abdominal adiposity; higher blood pressure; possible earlier-onset cardiovascular disease; possible attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; autism spectrum disorder. |

**Preconception plan**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prior to pregnancy | Optimize modifiable risk factors (e.g. BMI, diet, physical activity). Screen glycaemia in high-risk women. For pre-existing DM: maintain HbA1c below 6% with appropriate drugs (insulin and metformin). Screen for complications. | (same as left) |
| During pregnancy | Healthy diet and regular exercise unless there are obstetric contraindications. Possible personalized gestational weight gain. High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception screening positive). Follow the protocol for all at 24-28 weeks according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria. Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if sugars are well controlled; if poorly controlled, consult a specialist on timing of delivery. Consider steroids for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated. If steroids are given at any point in pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control; insulin therapy is advised. Aim for blood glucose 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery. Anticipate maternal and fetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions. | (same as left) |
| Postpartum | Early postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status. Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification. Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring. | (same as left) |

text:
### Gestational DM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule: metformin and insulin (starting dose, titration, timing, maximum), glucose targets and postpartum

**Metformin (oral, first line)**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin 500 mg | Lifestyle measures failed after 1-2 weeks; FBG ≥5.3 or 2-hr PPG ≥6.7 mmol/L | 500 mg once daily | Add 500 mg every 1-2 weeks as tolerated | With evening meal | 2000-2500 mg/day in 2-3 divided doses |
| Metformin (week 2) | Targets not met on 500 mg daily | 500 mg twice daily | Increase to 3x daily if still not at target by week 3 | Morning + evening meal | ~46% will still require insulin: reassess every 1-2 weeks |

**Insulin (injectable, gold standard)**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NPH insulin (Humulin N / Insulatard) | Fasting hyperglycaemia: FBG ≥5.3 mmol/L despite metformin | 0.1-0.2 units/kg at bedtime | Increase by 2 units every 3 days until FBG <5.3 mmol/L | Bedtime (22:00-23:00) | Formulary standard in SA & Eswatini public sector |
| Regular insulin (Actrapid / Humulin R) | Postprandial hyperglycaemia: 2-hr PPG ≥6.7 mmol/L | 4 units before highest-carb meal | Increase by 2 units every 3 days until 2-hr PPG <6.7 mmol/L | 30 min before meal | Extend to all 3 meals if multiple postprandial readings elevated |
| Basal-bolus (NPH + regular) | Both fasting & postprandial elevated | NPH 0.1-0.2 u/kg bedtime + 4 u regular before meals | Titrate each component separately; 2 units every 3 days | NPH at bedtime; regular 30 min pre-meal | Most physiological regimen; preferred for poorly controlled GDM |
| Insulin (specialist) | Severe: FBG ≥7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis | 0.2-0.3 u/kg/day total; split 2/3 AM + 1/3 PM (NPH) | Adjust based on full daily glucose profile | Split dose AM + bedtime | Refer to specialist (Mbabane GH or RFM Hospital in Eswatini) |

**Glucose targets & monitoring**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Targets | Fasting BG < 5.3 mmol/L; 1-hr postprandial < 7.8 mmol/L; 2-hr postprandial < 6.7 mmol/L | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |

**Postpartum**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All agents | Discontinue ALL pharmacotherapy at delivery | — | 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum to screen for persistent T2DM | — | Annual fasting glucose screening recommended long-term |

text:
### Drug interactions between antidiabetic agents and antiretrovirals (ARVs) (source: University of Liverpool hiv-druginteractions.org)

Diabetes in HIV: a dose adjustment of metformin should be considered when co-administering DTG with metformin to maintain glycaemic control. Monitor renal function and blood glucose when metformin and DTG are co-administered; patients with moderate renal impairment may be at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin concentrations.

| Antidiabetic agent | TDF/TAF | AZT | 3TC | FTC | EFV | NVP | DTG | LPV/r | ATV/r | DRV/r |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ CAUTION: metformin levels increased (limit metformin to 1,000 mg/day; monitor renal function) | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction |
| Glibenclamide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glipizide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliquidone | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliclazide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glimepiride | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |

Key: no interaction. Potential interaction with increased (↑) or decreased (↓) levels of the sulfonylurea, which may require dose adjustment: monitor blood glucose and adjust the sulfonylurea dosage as needed. CAUTION when co-administering metformin with DTG: metformin levels are increased and dose reduction of metformin should be considered. The US prescribing information recommends limiting the total daily dose of metformin to 1,000 mg when co-administered with DTG. Renal monitoring is recommended, as PLHIV with renal impairment are at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin levels in the presence of DTG.
*Essential medicines list included atenolol, metoprolol, carvedilol as alternatives (as printed under the table). Refer to National HIV Management Guidelines.

text:
### Drug interactions between antidiabetic agents and antiretrovirals (ARVs) (source: University of Liverpool hiv-druginteractions.org)

Diabetes in HIV: a dose adjustment of metformin should be considered when co-administering DTG with metformin to maintain glycaemic control. Monitor renal function and blood glucose when metformin and DTG are co-administered; patients with moderate renal impairment may be at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin concentrations.

| Antidiabetic agent | TDF/TAF | AZT | 3TC | FTC | EFV | NVP | DTG | LPV/r | ATV/r | DRV/r |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ CAUTION: metformin levels increased (limit metformin to 1,000 mg/day; monitor renal function) | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction |
| Glibenclamide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glipizide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliquidone | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliclazide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glimepiride | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |

Key: no interaction. Potential interaction with increased (↑) or decreased (↓) levels of the sulfonylurea, which may require dose adjustment: monitor blood glucose and adjust the sulfonylurea dosage as needed. CAUTION when co-administering metformin with DTG: metformin levels are increased and dose reduction of metformin should be considered. The US prescribing information recommends limiting the total daily dose of metformin to 1,000 mg when co-administered with DTG. Renal monitoring is recommended, as PLHIV with renal impairment are at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin levels in the presence of DTG.
*Essential medicines list included atenolol, metoprolol, carvedilol as alternatives (as printed under the table). Refer to National HIV Management Guidelines.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes in Special Populations > Diabetic emergencies in special populations
text:
### Diabetic emergencies (DKA/HHS) in special populations: HIV/TB co-infection, resource-limited settings, pregnancy, elderly

Diabetes and TB: anti-TB drugs can influence the metabolism of anti-diabetic medications. Rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 and increases the metabolism of most oral hypoglycaemic agents, which may worsen hyperglycaemia. Isoniazid inhibits cytochrome P450 and prolongs the effect of oral anti-diabetic drugs. Bedaquiline is also an enzyme inducer and reduces the effect of antidiabetic drugs.

| Population | Considerations |
| --- | --- |
| HIV/TB co-infection | Screen for HIV if status unknown (rapid test on admission). Immune reconstitution can unmask T1DM. ARVs (especially older PI-based) can cause insulin resistance. Opportunistic infections (PCP, cryptococcal, TB) are common DKA precipitants. Maintain ARTs during crisis; liaise with HIV team. |
| Resource-limited settings | No blood ketones: use urine ketones (≥2+ = significant). No VBG: treat on clinical picture + glucose + ketones. No syringe pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml) + drip control. No 0.45% NaCl: use 0.9% NaCl throughout with closer monitoring. Validate POC glucose meters for high glucose ranges >30 mmol/L. |
| Pregnancy | DKA can occur at lower glucose (euglycaemic DKA in pregnancy). Involve obstetric team immediately. Fetal monitoring from 24 weeks onwards. Higher insulin requirements: do not underdose. Avoid bicarbonate unless pH <7.0. |
| Elderly patients (HHS) | Reduced physiological reserve: higher risk of fluid overload. More gradual fluid replacement over 48-72 hours. Increased thromboembolic risk: early LMWH prophylaxis. Exclude silent MI, stroke, UTI, pneumonia as precipitant. Assess cognition, falls risk, social support before discharge. |

text:
### Risk factors for osteoporosis and fragility fractures (lifestyle, genetic, diseases, miscellaneous)

| Category | Risk factors |
| --- | --- |
| Lifestyle factors | Alcohol (two or more drinks per day)\*\*; smoking\*\*; low calcium intake; inadequate physical activity; immobilisation; vitamin D insufficiency; malnutrition; low body mass (BMI < 20)\*\*; falling; high salt/protein intake; high caffeine intake; excessive exercise; excess vitamin A; vitamin C, K, B6 and B12 deficiencies; trace element deficiencies |
| Genetic and ethnic factors | Elderly females\*\*; white, Asian and mixed race; family history of hip fracture\*\*; osteogenesis imperfecta; Marfan syndrome; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; haemochromatosis; porphyria; homocystinuria; idiopathic hypercalciuria; Gaucher's disease; Riley-Day syndrome; Menkes disease |

**Diseases**

| Category | Risk factors |
| --- | --- |
| Hypogonadism | Premature menopause; anorexia nervosa/bulimia; athlete's amenorrhoea; delayed puberty; Turner's syndrome; Klinefelter's syndrome; Kallmann's syndrome |
| Gastrointestinal disorders | Gastric bypass; coeliac disease; gastrectomy; inflammatory bowel disease; chronic liver disease; pancreatic disease |
| Endocrinopathies | Cushing's syndrome; diabetes mellitus; hyperthyroidism; acromegaly; Addison's disease; prolactinoma |
| Haematological disorders | Multiple myeloma; systemic mastocytosis; thalassaemia; leukaemia and lymphomas; sickle cell disease; haemophilia |
| Rheumatology and immunology | Rheumatoid arthritis\*\*; psoriasis; systemic lupus erythematosus; ankylosing spondylitis |
| Miscellaneous | Alcoholism; malignancy; fracture after age 40 years\*\*; parenteral nutrition; amyloidosis; sarcoidosis; post-transplant bone disease; organ failure (lung, liver, kidney, heart); pregnancy-associated osteoporosis; bone-toxic drugs (see drugs table) |

x = do at this visit; blank = not routinely (some items, e.g. 25OHD, nystagmus, eGFR and ECG, have no marks in the PDF).
*Vertigo assessment: clinician may use any of: (1) the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre: the patient sits at the edge of the bed and the examiner turns the patient's head 30-45 degrees to the side being tested; the patient keeps eyes open on a stable point and then quickly lies supine with the neck hyperextended; horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive test (warn the patient it can induce vertigo). (2) Orthostatic blood pressure testing: a drop in systolic BP of more than 20 mmHg from lying to standing is significant for a postural drop (dehydration or autonomic dysfunction, which can cause vertigo). (3) Head impulse test: the patient looks at the examiner's nose and the examiner quickly turns the head 10-20 degrees; it is abnormal if the eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate on the examiner's nose (disrupted vestibulo-ocular reflex).

*Vertigo assessment: clinician may use any of: (1) the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre: the patient sits at the edge of the bed and the examiner turns the patient's head 30-45 degrees to the side being tested; the patient keeps eyes open on a stable point and then quickly lies supine with the neck hyperextended; horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive test (warn the patient it can induce vertigo). (2) Orthostatic blood pressure testing: a drop in systolic BP of more than 20 mmHg from lying to standing is significant for a postural drop (dehydration or autonomic dysfunction, which can cause vertigo). (3) Head impulse test: the patient looks at the examiner's nose and the examiner quickly turns the head 10-20 degrees; it is abnormal if the eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate on the examiner's nose (disrupted vestibulo-ocular reflex).

text:
### Classification of osteoporosis by bone mineral density (BMD) T-score

| Definition | Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Normal | BMD or BMC value (measured with DXA at either the spine, total hip or femur neck) within 1 SD of the young adult reference mean (T-score\* at or above -1.0) |
| Low bone mass | BMD or BMC value more than 1 SD but less than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean (osteopenia; T-score between -1.0 and -2.5) |
| Osteoporosis | BMD or BMC value 2.5 SD or more below the young adult mean |
| Severe osteoporosis | BMD or BMC value more than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean, plus one or more fragility fractures |

**Note:** These criteria were updated in 2008 and differ from those proposed by the WHO in 1994 by specifying a single reference site (the femoral neck) to measure BMD, providing a young normal reference range for women and men (the NHANES III reference data for femoral neck measurements in women aged 20-29 years), and by accommodating diagnostic criteria for men. *When standard deviation (SD) units are used in relation to the young healthy adult population, this is referred to as the T-score.

text:
### Algorithm for the management of osteoporosis in post-menopausal women and men aged 50 years and older

Clinical risk factors (CRFs): advanced age; prior fracture; family history; excessive leanness (printed 'excessive learners'); diet/alcohol/smoking; fall propensity; secondary osteoporoses.

Start: women and men with CRFs. Prior osteoporotic fracture?
- Yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
- No: measure BMD. By T-score:
  - T-score ≤ -2.5: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
  - T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 (printed '< -10 to > -2.5'; consider FRAX):
      - > 75 years: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
      - 65-75 years + ≥ 2 CRFs: yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis; no: individualised assessment of CRFs + BMD.
      - > 60 years: individualised assessment of CRFs + BMD.
    Individualised assessment outcome: yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis; uncertain (?): bone turnover markers (BTMs) or reassess in 24 months; no: lifestyle changes only.
  - T-score ≥ -1.0: lifestyle changes only.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Osteoporosis and Fragility Fractures > Pharmacological management of osteoporosis
text:
### Pharmacological management of osteoporosis: drug classes, typical dosage and common side effects

Non-pharmacological management: postmenopausal women and men aged ≥50 years with osteoporosis or at risk of fragility fracture are recommended: a healthy, nutrient-rich balanced diet; adequate calcium intake (minimum 700 mg daily), preferably from diet or otherwise by supplementation; vitamin D supplements of at least 800 IU/day if vitamin D insufficiency or risk factors for it are identified; regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise tailored to the individual; advice on smoking and alcohol cessation; a falls assessment for all patients with osteoporosis and fragility fractures, with exercise programmes to improve balance for those at risk.

**Bisphosphonates**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alendronate (Fosamax) | 70 mg once weekly or 10 mg daily | Oesophageal irritation, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, abdominal pain |
| Risedronate (Actonel) | 35 mg once weekly or 150 mg once monthly | Abdominal pain, musculoskeletal pain, nausea |
| Ibandronate (Boniva) | 150 mg once monthly | Gastrointestinal irritation, musculoskeletal pain |
| Zoledronic acid (Reclast) | 5 mg once annually as an intravenous infusion | Flu-like symptoms, renal impairment, hypocalcaemia |

**Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs)**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raloxifene (Evista) | 60 mg daily | Hot flashes, leg cramps, increased risk of blood clots |

**Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conjugated estrogens (Premarin) | Dosage varies | Increased risk of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, and other side effects |
| Calcitonin (Miacalcin) | Typically 200 IU daily as nasal spray | Nasal irritation, epistaxis (nosebleeds), flushing |

**Parathyroid hormone analogs**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Teriparatide (Forteo) | 20 mcg once daily (subcutaneous) | Dizziness, leg cramps, injection site reactions |
| Abaloparatide (Tymlos) | 80 mcg once daily (subcutaneous) | Hypercalcaemia, dizziness, nausea, headache |

**Monoclonal antibodies**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Denosumab (Prolia) | 60 mg once every six months (subcutaneous) | Infections, back pain, dermatitis, hypocalcaemia |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hypothyroidism > Diagnostic criteria
text:
### Hypothyroidism symptoms by system affected (diagnostic criteria)

The symptoms of hypothyroidism depend on the deficiency of thyroid hormone, but can include the following. Investigations: thyroid hormone profile. Diagnosis: may be primary or secondary hypothyroidism.

| System affected | Common symptoms |
| --- | --- |
| General & metabolic | Fatigue; weight gain; trouble tolerating cold; slowed heart rate; increased cholesterol levels |
| Skin, hair & nails | Dry, rough skin; dry or thinning hair; hair loss |
| Musculoskeletal | Joint pain; muscle pain or weakness |
| Reproductive (female) | Heavy or irregular menstrual periods; fertility problems |
| Neurological & psychological | Depression; memory loss |
| Gastrointestinal & voice | Constipation; hoarse voice |

### Congenital hypothyroidism: clinical features by category

| Category | Features |
| --- | --- |
| General | Lethargy, somnolence, delayed physical and mental development, subnormal temperature |
| Skin/hair | Dry skin, coarse and scanty hair |
| Facial/head | Wide open fontanelles, enlarged tongue (macroglossia), periorbital oedema, coarse cry, hoarse voice, goitre |

| Cardiovascular | Bradycardia |
| Abdomen | Abdominal distension, umbilical hernia, constipation |
| Extremities | Oedema of extremities and genitals |
| Haematologic | Anaemia |
| Respiratory | Apnoeic episodes |
| Feeding | Feeding difficulties |
| Other | Prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hypothyroidism in Older Children and Adolescents > Pharmacological treatment
text:
### Levothyroxine dose by age for hypothyroidism in children and adolescents (oral, once daily on an empty stomach)

Hypothyroidism in older children and adolescents: low growth velocity or short stature with short limbs and a normal or elevated BMI; subtle features include cold intolerance, dry skin, brittle hair, pallor and myxoedema. Investigations: elevated TSH and low thyroxine. Levothyroxine, oral, once daily on an empty stomach. Refer all cases for investigation and initiation of therapy. (Neonates with congenital hypothyroidism: levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg once daily, started ideally within the first three weeks of life.)

| Age group | Levothyroxine dose |
| --- | --- |
| 1-6 months | 8-10 mcg/kg |
| 6-12 months | 6-8 mcg/kg |
| 1-5 years | 5-6 mcg/kg |
| 6-12 years | 4-5 mcg/kg |
| >12 years | 2-3 mcg/kg |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism
text:
### Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism (by radioactive iodine uptake)

Primary hyperthyroidism: ↓ TSH, ↑ free T4, ↑ total T3. Next: radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU).
- Diffuse uptake: homogeneous: Graves' disease; heterogeneous: toxic multinodular goitre.
- Focal uptake: functioning adenoma.
- No uptake: measure serum thyroglobulin: low (↓): thyrotoxicosis factitia; high (↑): thyroiditis, iodine load, or struma ovarii.

### Antithyroid drug therapy for hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm: medicines, dosing and comments

| Medicine | Dosing | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propylthiouracil\* (D) | 500-1000 mg load, then 250 mg 4-hourly | Blocks new hormone synthesis; blocks T4-to-T3 conversion. Breastfeeding clients: propylthiouracil (up to a maximum dose of 450 mg/day). |
| Carbimazole (C) | 40-60 mg/day | Blocks new hormone synthesis. Breastfeeding clients: carbimazole (up to maximum 15 mg/day). |
| Propranolol (A) | 60-80 mg every 4 hours | Consider invasive monitoring in congestive heart failure patients. Blocks T4-to-T3 conversion in high doses. Alternative medicine: esmolol infusion. |
| Iodine (saturated solution of potassium iodide) (B) | 5 drops (0.25 mL or 250 mg) (PO) 6-hourly | Do not start until 1 hour after antithyroid medicines. Blocks new hormone synthesis; blocks thyroid hormone release. |
| Hydrocortisone (A) | 300 mg intravenous load, then 100 mg 8-hourly | May block T4-to-T3 conversion. Prophylaxis against relative adrenal insufficiency. Alternative medicine: dexamethasone. |

**Note:** Note: in thyroid storm, propylthiouracil is preferred to carbimazole.

Letters A-D after each medicine are the evidence/medicine codes as printed. *No footnote for the asterisk on propylthiouracil is printed.

text:
### Interpreting TSH and FT4/FT3 results (thyroid function test flowchart)

Start with TSH.

TSH low:
- FT4 and/or FT3 high (printed 'Nor FT4 and/or FT3 high'): primary hyperthyroidism. Perform test for TRAb/TSI; consider ordering thyroid scintigraphy. Repeat TFT in four weeks to determine course or impact of treatment. Specialist referral*.
- FT4 and FT3 normal*: subclinical/mild hyperthyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 in 1-3 months; may require further investigation.
- FT4 and/or FT3 low: discordant: non-thyroidal illness; central hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 and follow to assess trend; if persistently abnormal, refer for further investigation.

TSH normal: thyroid dysfunction excluded.

TSH high:
- FT4 low: primary hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH and FT4; check anti-TPO; treat with levothyroxine.
- FT4 normal: subclinical/mild hypothyroidism. Repeat in 1-3 months; check anti-TPO antibody; monitor TFT annually if stable; consider treatment with levothyroxine*.
- FT4 high: discordant: TSHoma; thyroid hormone resistance; assay interference. Repeat TSH and FT4 to assess trend; refer for further investigation.

text:
### Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) for diagnosis of thyroid storm: criteria, points and interpretation

Thyroid storm/thyrotoxic crisis is a rare but potentially life-threatening syndrome of exaggerated hyperthyroidism: hyperthermia, severe tachycardia with or without cardiac failure, severe agitation, possible jaundice, and mental disorientation, culminating in stupor and coma.

| Category | Feature | Criteria (points) | Score range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thermoregulatory dysfunction | Temperature (°C) | 37.2-37.7: 5; 37.8-38.3: 10; 38.4-38.8: 15; 38.9-39.4: 20; 39.5-39.9: 25; ≥40.0: 30 | 5-30 |
| Central nervous system effects | Manifestations | Mild (agitation): 10; moderate (delirium, psychosis, extreme lethargy): 20; severe (seizure, coma): 30 | 0-30 |
| Gastrointestinal-hepatic dysfunction | Symptoms | Moderate (diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain): 10; severe (jaundice): 20 | 0-20 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Tachycardia (bpm) | 90-109: 5; 110-119: 10; 120-129: 15; 130-139: 20; ≥140: 25 | 5-25 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Atrial fibrillation | Present: 10 | 0-10 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Congestive heart failure | Mild (pedal oedema): 5; moderate (bibasilar rales): 10; severe (pulmonary oedema): 15 | 0-15 |
| Precipitating event | Trigger (e.g., infection, surgery, trauma, withdrawal of antithyroid drugs) | Present: 10 | 0-10 |

**Note:** Interpretation of total score: ≥45: thyroid storm highly likely; 25-44: impending storm; <25: thyroid storm unlikely.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Management of thyroid storm > Recognition and management (flowchart)
text:
### Thyroid storm: recognition and management (flowchart)

1. Suspect thyroid storm (BWPS ≥45).
2. Identify precipitant(s).
3. Initial stabilization (ABC). Propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole.
4. Block thyroid hormone synthesis (≥ 1 h after ATD): Lugol's iodine 8 drops PO q6-8h, or NaI IV 0.25-0.5 g q6h.
5. Block peripheral effects: propranolol 60-80 mg OG 6-hourly, or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h.
6. Continuous monitoring & support: ECG, vitals, fluid balance, electrolytes. Adjust therapy as needed.

In addition to general supportive measures, therapy should be directed at the thyroid gland and the hypermetabolism and tachycardia. Patients should be monitored in an intensive or high care setting. The underlying precipitant should be actively treated and managed. Prevention is key: correct thyroid function before elective surgery.

text:
### Thyroid storm treatment steps: therapeutic targets, drugs and doses

| Step | Therapeutic target | Drug / intervention | Dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Block thyroid hormone synthesis | Antithyroid drugs (ATDs) | Propylthiouracil (PTU): 500-1000 mg loading, then 250 mg q4h; preferred early as it inhibits T4-to-T3 conversion. Methimazole: 60-80 mg/day if PTU unavailable. | Start immediately on diagnosis |
| Block hormone release (give ≥1 hr after ATD) | Iodine therapy | Lugol's iodine: 8 drops q6-8h. Sodium iodide IV: 0.25-0.5 g q6h. Administer ≥1 hr after ATD to avoid iodine-fuelled synthesis. | Reduces preformed hormone release |
| Block peripheral effects | Beta-blockade; corticosteroid therapy | Propranolol: 60-80 mg PO q6h or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3 doses); esmolol IV infusion is an alternative in heart failure. Hydrocortisone: 100 mg IV q8h (reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and prevents adrenal crisis). | Controls adrenergic effects; protects against adrenal failure |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy > Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
text:
### Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (flowchart)

Two entry points:
- Known hyperthyroidism on ATD and wishing to conceive/pregnant: switch to a 'dose titration' regimen if on 'block and replace'. Use PTU pre-conception and in the 1st trimester; use CBZ (carbimazole) thereafter.
- New diagnosis of hyperthyroidism during pregnancy: commence anti-thyroid medication: PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter.

Both: refer to endocrine physician. Then two parallel tracks:

Track 1 - check TFTs every 4 weeks (and LFTs every 4 weeks if on PTU):
- Free T4 above normal reference range: increase dose of ATD.
- Free T4 at or just above upper end of normal reference range: continue on current dose of ATD.
- Free T4 below upper end of normal reference range: decrease dose of ATD.
Repeat the 4-weekly checks throughout pregnancy. TFTs to be checked 6-8 weeks post-partum (printed 'at first ante-natal check').

Track 2 - check TRAb at 22 weeks and 36 weeks. If TRAb > 2-3 times the upper limit of normal: obstetric ultrasound for monitoring for fetal thyrotoxicosis.

Reference: Girling JC. Thyroid disease in pregnancy. The Obstetrician and Gynaecologist 2008; 10:237-243.
